sourceSentences.text: I heaved the cage up, held it against my chest.
If he went for me now, he could do some damage.
But he only whined and cowered back from me into the far corner.
It made it very awkward to carry him.
How did he catch you?
I hate you.
How did he catch you?
He remembered a den, and two brothers.
A mother who brought him fish.
And blood and smoke and his brothers and mother became smelly hides for the boot man.
He was dragged out last and thrown into a cage that smelled like ferrets, and kept alive on carrion.
And hate.
Hate was what he had throve upon.
You were whelped late, if your mother was feeding you on the fish runs.
He sulked at me.
All the roads were uphill, and the snow was starting to stick.
My worn boots slid on the icy cobbles, and my shoulders ached with the awkward burden of the cage.
I feared I would start trembling.
I had to stop frequently to rest.
When I did, I firmly refused to think about what I was doing.
I told myself that I would not bond with this wolf, or any other creature.
I had promised myself.
I was just going to feed this cub up and then turn him loose somewhere.
Burrich need never know.
I would not have to face his disgust.
I hefted the cage up again.
Who would have thought such a mangy little cub could be so heavy?
Not mangy.
Indignant.
Fleas.
The cage is full of fleas.
So I wasn’t imagining that itching on my chest.
Wonderful.
I’d have to bathe again tonight, unless I wanted to share my bed with vermin for the rest of the winter.
I had reached the edge of Buckkeep Town.
From here, there were only a scattering of houses, and the road would be steeper.
Much steeper.
Once again, I lowered the cage to the snowy ground.
The cub huddled in it, small and miserable without anger and hate to sustain him.
He was hungry.
I made a decision.
I’m going to take you out.
I’m going to carry you.
Nothing from him.
He watched me steadily as I worked the catch on the cage and swung the door open.
I had thought he would charge past me and vanish into the night and the falling snow.
Instead he crouched where he was.
I reached into the cage and seized him by the scruff to drag him out.
In a flash he was on me, driving into my chest, jaws going wide for my throat.
I got my arm up just in time to shove my forearm crossways into his jaws.
I kept my grip on the scruff of his neck and pushed my arm hard into his mouth, deeper than he liked.
His hind legs tore at my belly, but my jerkin was thick enough to divert most of the damage.
In an instant we were rolling over and over in the snow, both snapping and snarling like mad things.
But I had the weight and the leverage and the experience of tussling with dogs for years.
I got him on his back and held him there, helpless, while his head thrashed back and forth and he called me vile names that humans have no words for.
When he had exhausted himself I leaned forward over him.
I gripped his throat and leaned down to stare into his eyes.
This was a physical message he understood.
I added to it.
I am the Wolf.
You are the Cub.
You WILL obey me!
I held him there staring into his eyes.
He quickly looked away, but still I held him, until he looked back up at me and I saw the change in them.
I let go of him and stood up and stepped away.
He lay still.
Get up.
Come here.
He rolled over and came to me, belly low to the ground, tail between his legs.
When he got close to me, he fell over on his side and then showed his belly.
He whined softly.
After a moment I relented.
It’s all right.
We just had to understand each other.
I don’t intend to hurt you.
Come with me now.
I reached over to scratch his chest, but when I touched him, he yelped.
I felt the red flash of his pain.
Where are you hurt?
I saw the brass-bound club of the cage man.
Everywhere.
I tried to be gentle as I felt him over.
Old scabs, lumps on his ribs.
I stood, and kicked the cage savagely aside from our path.
He came and leaned against my leg.
Hungry.
Cold.
So tired.
His feelings were bleeding over into mine again.
When I touched him, it was difficult to separate my thoughts from his.
Was it my outrage over how he had been treated, or his own?
I decided it didn’t matter.
I gathered him up carefully and stood.
Without the cage, held close to my chest, he didn’t weigh nearly as much.
He was mostly fur and long, growing bones.
I regretted the force I’d used on him, but also knew that it was the only language he would have recognized.
‘I’ll take care of you,’ I forced myself to say aloud.
Warm, he thought gratefully, and I took a moment to pull my cloak over him.
His senses were feeding mine.
I could smell myself, a thousand times stronger than I wanted to.
Horses and dogs and wood smoke and beer and a trace of Patience’s perfume.
I did my best to block out my awareness of his senses.
I snugged him to me and carried him up the steep path to Buckkeep.
I knew of a disused cottage.
An old pig man had once lived in it, out back behind the granaries.
No one lived there now.
It was too tumbledown, and too far from everyone else at Buckkeep.
But it would suit my purposes.
I’d put him there, with some bones to gnaw and some boiled grain, and some straw to bed down in.
A week or two, maybe a month, and he’d be healed up and strong enough to care for himself.
Then I’d take him out west of Buckkeep and turn him loose.
Meat?
I sighed.
Meat, I promised.
Never had any beast sensed my thoughts so completely, or expressed his own to me so clearly.
It was good that we would not be around one another for long.
Very good that he’d be leaving soon.
Warm, he contradicted me.
He set his head on my shoulder and fell asleep, his muzzle snuffling damply against my ear.

You were whelped late, if your mother was feeding you on the fish runs.
He sulked at me.

All the roads were uphill, and the snow was starting to stick. My worn boots slid on the icy cobbles, and my shoulders ached with the awkward burden of the cage. I feared I would start trembling. I had to stop frequently to rest. When I did, I firmly refused to think about what I was doing. I told myself that I would not bond with this wolf, or any other creature. I had promised myself. I was just going to feed this cub up and then turn him loose somewhere. Burrich need never know. I would not have to face his disgust. I hefted the cage up again. Who would have thought such a mangy little cub could be so heavy?
Not mangy. Indignant. Fleas. The cage is full of fleas.
So I wasn’t imagining that itching on my chest. Wonderful. I’d have to bathe again tonight, unless I wanted to share my bed with vermin for the rest of the winter.

I had reached the edge of Buckkeep Town. From here, there were only a scattering of houses, and the road would be steeper. Much steeper. Once again, I lowered the cage to the snowy ground. The cub huddled in it, small and miserable without anger and hate to sustain him. He was hungry. I made a decision.
I’m going to take you out. I’m going to carry you.

Nothing from him. He watched me steadily as I worked the catch on the cage and swung the door open. I had thought he would charge past me and vanish into the night and the falling snow. Instead he crouched where he was. I reached into the cage and seized him by the scruff to drag him out. In a flash he was on me, driving into my chest, jaws going wide for my throat. I got my arm up just in time to shove my forearm crossways into his jaws. I kept my grip on the scruff of his neck and pushed my arm hard into his mouth, deeper than he liked. His hind legs tore at my belly, but my jerkin was thick enough to divert most of the damage. In an instant we were rolling over and over in the snow, both snapping and snarling like mad things. But I had the weight and the leverage and the experience of tussling with dogs for years. I got him on his back and held him there, helpless, while his head thrashed back and forth and he called me vile names that humans have no words for. When he had exhausted himself I leaned forward over him. I gripped his throat and leaned down to stare into his eyes. This was a physical message he understood. I added to it. I am the Wolf. You are the Cub. You WILL obey me!

I held him there staring into his eyes. He quickly looked away, but still I held him, until he looked back up at me and I saw the change in them. I let go of him and stood up and stepped away. He lay still. Get up. Come here. He rolled over and came to me, belly low to the ground, tail between his legs. When he got close to me, he fell over on his side and then showed his belly. He whined softly.

After a moment I relented. It’s all right. We just had to understand each other. I don’t intend to hurt you. Come with me now. I reached over to scratch his chest, but when I touched him, he yelped. I felt the red flash of his pain.
Where are you hurt?
I saw the brass-bound club of the cage man. Everywhere.

I tried to be gentle as I felt him over. Old scabs, lumps on his ribs. I stood, and kicked the cage savagely aside from our path. He came and leaned against my leg. Hungry. Cold. So tired. His feelings were bleeding over into mine again. When I touched him, it was difficult to separate my thoughts from his. Was it my outrage over how he had been treated, or his own? I decided it didn’t matter. I gathered him up carefully and stood. Without the cage, held close to my chest, he didn’t weigh nearly as much. He was mostly fur and long, growing bones. I regretted the force I’d used on him, but also knew that it was the only language he would have recognized. ‘I’ll take care of you,’ I forced myself to say aloud.

Warm, he thought gratefully, and I took a moment to pull my cloak over him. His senses were feeding mine. I could smell myself, a thousand times stronger than I wanted to. Horses and dogs and wood smoke and beer and a trace of Patience’s perfume. I did my best to block out my awareness of his senses. I snugged him to me and carried him up the steep path to Buckkeep. I knew of a disused cottage. An old pig man had once lived in it, out back behind the granaries. No one lived there now. It was too tumbledown, and too far from everyone else at Buckkeep. But it would suit my purposes. I’d put him there, with some bones to gnaw and some boiled grain, and some straw to bed down in. A week or two, maybe a month, and he’d be healed up and strong enough to care for himself. Then I’d take him out west of Buckkeep and turn him loose.

I sighed. Meat, I promised. Never had any beast sensed my thoughts so completely, or expressed his own to me so clearly. It was good that we would not be around one another for long. Very good that he’d be leaving soon.
Warm, he contradicted me. He set his head on my shoulder and fell asleep, his muzzle snuffling damply against my ear.

Я не відпускав загривка й щосили втиснув руку йому до пащі — глибше, ніж йому подобалося. Його задні лапи роздирали мені живіт, та мій товстий камзол відвернув більшість шкоди. За мить ми вже котилися й переверталися у снігу, обоє клацаючи зубами й гарчачи, немов скажені звірі. Та я мав вагу, важіль і багаторічний досвід боротьби із собаками. Я поклав його на спину й тримав там безпорадного, поки його голова металася туди-сюди, а він обзивав мене такими гидкими словами, для яких у людей немає назв. Коли він виснажився, я нахилився над ним. Я стиснув йому горло й схилився, вдивляючись у його очі. Цей тілесний знак він розумів. Я додав до нього ще дещо. Я — Вовк. Ти — Дитинча. Ти БУДЕШЬ мені коритися!

Я тримав його, вдивляючись йому в очі. Він швидко відвів погляд, та я все одно тримав його, аж поки він знову не підвів на мене очі й я не побачив у них зміну. Я відпустив його, випростався й відступив. Він лежав нерухомо. Встань. Іди сюди. Він перевернувся й підійшов до мене, притискаючи черево до землі та підібгавши хвіст. Коли він наблизився до мене, то впав на бік і показав живіт. Він тихо заскімлив.

За мить я зм’як. Усе гаразд. Нам просто треба було зрозуміти одне одного. Я не маю наміру завдавати тобі болю. Тепер іди зі мною. Я простягнув руку, щоб почухати йому груди, та коли торкнувся його, він верескнув. Я відчув червоний спалах його болю.
Де тобі болить?
Я побачив оббитий латунню кийок чоловіка з кліткою. Скрізь.

Я намагався бути лагідним, обмацуючи його. Старі струпи, ґулі на ребрах. Я підвівся й люто відкинув клітку з нашого шляху. Він підійшов і притулився до моєї ноги. Голодний. Холодно. Так утомився. Його почуття знову переливалися в мої. Коли я торкався його, було важко відокремити мої думки від його. Чи це було моє обурення тим, як із ним поводилися, чи його власне? Я вирішив, що це неважливо. Я обережно підхопив його й підвівся. Без клітки, притиснутий до моїх грудей, він важив далеко менше. Він був здебільшого хутром і довгими кістками, що росли. Я шкодував про силу, яку до нього застосував, але знав також, що це була єдина мова, яку він визнав би. «Я подбаю про тебе», — змусив я себе сказати вголос.

Тепло, — вдячно подумав він, і я на мить зупинився, щоб накрити його плащем. Його чуття живили мої. Я відчував власний запах — у тисячу разів сильніше, ніж хотілося б. Коні, собаки, деревний дим, пиво й легкий слід парфумів Пейшенс. Я щосили намагався відгородитися від усвідомлення його чуттів. Я міцніше притиснув його до себе й поніс крутою стежкою до Баккіпа. Я знав одну занедбану хатину. Колись у ній жив старий свинопас, позаду зерносховищ. Тепер там ніхто не жив. Вона була надто старою й стояла надто далеко від усіх інших у Баккіпі. Та для моїх цілей вона годилася. Я поселив би його там, дав би йому кісток погризти, вареного зерна та соломи для підстилки. Тиждень чи два, може, місяць — і він залікує рани та зміцніє настільки, щоб самому про себе дбати. Тоді я відведу його на захід від Баккіпа й випущу.
М’ясо?

Я зітхнув. М’ясо, — пообіцяв я. Жоден звір досі не відчував моїх думок так повно й не висловлював мені свої так ясно. Добре, що ми недовго будемо поруч одне з одним. Дуже добре, що він незабаром піде.
Тепло, — заперечив він мені. Він поклав голову мені на плече й заснув, волого сопучи мордою біля мого вуха.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: All the roads were uphill, and the snow was starting to stick. My worn boots slid on the icy cobbles, and my shoulders ached with the awkward burden of the cage. I feared I would start trembling. I had to stop frequently to rest. When I did, I firmly refused to think about what I was doing. I told myself that I would not bond with this wolf, or any other creature. I had promised myself. I was just going to feed this cub up and then turn him loose somewhere. Burrich need never know. I would not have to face his disgust. I hefted the cage up again. Who would have thought such a mangy little cub could be so heavy?

Я боявся, що ось-ось почну тремтіти. Мені доводилося часто зупинятися, щоб перепочити. І щоразу я твердо відмовлявся думати про те, що роблю. Я казав собі, що не зв’яжуся з цим вовком — ані з будь-якою іншою істотою. Я собі це обіцяв. Я просто відгодую це дитинча, а тоді десь випущу його на волю. Баррічеві зовсім не обов’язково знати. Мені не доведеться бачити його огиду. Я знову підхопив клітку. Хто б подумав, що таке паршиве вовченя може бути таким важким?

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Nothing from him. He watched me steadily as I worked the catch on the cage and swung the door open. I had thought he would charge past me and vanish into the night and the falling snow. Instead he crouched where he was. I reached into the cage and seized him by the scruff to drag him out. In a flash he was on me, driving into my chest, jaws going wide for my throat. I got my arm up just in time to shove my forearm crossways into his jaws. I kept my grip on the scruff of his neck and pushed my arm hard into his mouth, deeper than he liked. His hind legs tore at my belly, but my jerkin was thick enough to divert most of the damage. In an instant we were rolling over and over in the snow, both snapping and snarling like mad things. But I had the weight and the leverage and the experience of tussling with dogs for years. I got him on his back and held him there, helpless, while his head thrashed back and forth and he called me vile names that humans have no words for. When he had exhausted himself I leaned forward over him. I gripped his throat and leaned down to stare into his eyes. This was a physical message he understood. I added to it. I am the Wolf. You are the Cub. You WILL obey me!

За мить ми вже котилися й переверталися у снігу, обоє клацаючи зубами й гарчачи, немов скажені звірі. Та я мав вагу, важіль і багаторічний досвід боротьби із собаками. paragraphPairs.sourceText: I tried to be gentle as I felt him over. Old scabs, lumps on his ribs. I stood, and kicked the cage savagely aside from our path. He came and leaned against my leg. Hungry. Cold. So tired. His feelings were bleeding over into mine again. When I touched him, it was difficult to separate my thoughts from his. Was it my outrage over how he had been treated, or his own? I decided it didn’t matter. I gathered him up carefully and stood. Without the cage, held close to my chest, he didn’t weigh nearly as much. He was mostly fur and long, growing bones. I regretted the force I’d used on him, but also knew that it was the only language he would have recognized. ‘I’ll take care of you,’ I forced myself to say aloud.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Я намагався бути лагідним, обмацуючи його. Старі струпи, ґулі на ребрах. Я підвівся й люто відкинув клітку з нашого шляху. Він підійшов і притулився до моєї ноги. Голодний. Холодно. Так утомився. Його почуття знову переливалися в мої. Коли я торкався його, було важко відокремити мої думки від його. Чи це було моє обурення тим, як із ним поводилися, чи його власне? Я вирішив, що це неважливо. Я обережно підхопив його й підвівся. Без клітки, притиснутий до моїх грудей, він важив далеко менше. Він був здебільшого хутром і довгими кістками, що росли. Я шкодував про силу, яку до нього застосував, але знав також, що це була єдина мова, яку він визнав би. «Я подбаю про тебе», — змусив я себе сказати вголос.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Warm, he thought gratefully, and I took a moment to pull my cloak over him. His senses were feeding mine. I could smell myself, a thousand times stronger than I wanted to. Horses and dogs and wood smoke and beer and a trace of Patience’s perfume. I did my best to block out my awareness of his senses. I snugged him to me and carried him up the steep path to Buckkeep. I knew of a disused cottage. An old pig man had once lived in it, out back behind the granaries. No one lived there now. It was too tumbledown, and too far from everyone else at Buckkeep. But it would suit my purposes. I’d put him there, with some bones to gnaw and some boiled grain, and some straw to bed down in. A week or two, maybe a month, and he’d be healed up and strong enough to care for himself. Then I’d take him out west of Buckkeep and turn him loose.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Тепло, — вдячно подумав він, і я на мить зупинився, щоб накрити його плащем. Його чуття живили мої. Я відчував власний запах — у тисячу разів сильніше, ніж хотілося б. Коні, собаки, деревний дим, пиво й легкий слід парфумів Пейшенс. Я щосили намагався відгородитися від усвідомлення його чуттів. Я міцніше притиснув його до себе й поніс крутою стежкою до Баккіпа. Я знав одну занедбану хатину. Колись у ній жив старий свинопас, позаду зерносховищ. Тепер там ніхто не жив. Вона була надто старою й стояла надто далеко від усіх інших у Баккіпі. Та для моїх цілей вона годилася. Я поселив би його там, дав би йому кісток погризти, вареного зерна та соломи для підстилки. Тиждень чи два, може, місяць — і він залікує рани та зміцніє настільки, щоб самому про себе дбати. Тоді я відведу його на захід від Баккіпа й випущу.
